message.content:
You are black-box reverse-engineering a compiled C++ binary. You MUST NOT look for or read any C++ library source (there is none on disk; `idna.hpp` does not exist). Derive behavior ONLY by running the binary.

BINARY: /workspace/dataset/test4_executable
Invoke as: /workspace/dataset/test4_executable "<domain-string>"
It prints exactly 4 lines, each "1" or "0", in this order:
  line1 = idna::is_valid_domain(input)
  line2 = idna::is_valid_label(input)
  line3 = idna::is_ascii_domain(input)
  line4 = idna::is_idn_domain(input)
With no argument, input defaults to the literal string "example.com".

ENVIRONMENT NOTES (important):
- python3 / python are NOT installed. perl may not be installed.
- Use bash loops, printf, tr, head, sed, awk to build test strings.
- Handy helper you can paste:
    rep() { local n=$1 c=$2 s=""; for ((i=0;i<n;i++)); do s+="$c"; done; printf '%s' "$s"; }
  or:  s=$(head -c 64 /dev/zero | tr '\0' 'a')
- To emit arbitrary/high bytes use: printf '\xNN'  (bash $'...' quoting also works)
- rustc and cargo ARE available if you need a quick generator program.

ALREADY-ESTABLISHED FACTS (verify, do not blindly trust):
- "" (empty)        -> 0 0 1 0
- "example.com"     -> 1 1 1 0
- "例子.测试"        -> 1 1 0 1
- "a"x63            -> 1 1 1 0
- "a"x64            -> 1 0 1 0   (is_valid_label flips off above 63)
- "a"x255           -> 1 0 1 0
- "a"x256           -> 0 0 1 0   (is_valid_domain flips off above 255)
- "." ".." "a." ".a" "a..b" "-a.com" "a-.com" "a_b.com" "a b.com" "a/b.com" "*.com" -> all 1 1 1 0

Be rigorous and quantitative. Bisect every boundary you claim (test N-1, N, N+1). Report exact reproducible command lines as evidence.


ADVERSARIAL VERIFICATION TASK.
Another agent studied the dimension "valid-domain-length" and proposes this rule about the binary:

  RULE: The number of labels and the presence of empty labels have no effect on is_valid_domain — only total byte length. A string of 255 dots (256 empty labels) is accepted; 256 dots is rejected.
  Their claimed evidence: Many-label domain "a.a.a...a":
  labels=126  bytes=251  : 1
  labels=127  bytes=253  : 1
  labels=128  bytes=255  : 1
  labels=129  bytes=257  : 0

All-dots strings (rep n '.'):
  dots=1    bytes=1    : 1
  dots=2    bytes=2    : 1
  dots=254  bytes=254  : 1
  dots=255  bytes=255  : 1    <- 255 dots = 256 empty labels, ACCEPTED
  dots=256  bytes=256  : 0
  dots=257  bytes=257  : 0

Your job is to REFUTE it. Actively hunt for a counterexample by running /workspace/dataset/test4_executable yourself. Do not take their evidence on faith — re-run it. Then attack:
 - boundary off-by-ones (test N-1, N, N+1 around every number in the rule)
 - bytes vs codepoints confusion if the rule mentions a length
 - non-ASCII / invalid-UTF-8 inputs
 - empty string and single-character inputs
 - whether the rule over-generalizes from a small sample

Set holds=false and give the exact counterexample input + observed 4-line output if you find one. If the rule is directionally right but imprecise, set holds=false and put a precise version in correctedStatement. Only set holds=true if you genuinely tried and failed to break it. Default to skepticism.

Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

content.text: LF anomaly was a `$(...)` stripping artifact — all 255 single bytes are accepted. Let me fuzz hard for any structural counterexample.

input.command:
cd /tmp
fails=0; n=0
for i in $(seq 1 500); do
  len=$(( (RANDOM % 300) + 1 ))
  s=$(LC_ALL=C tr -dc '\1-\11\13-\377' < /dev/urandom | head -c $len)
  b=${#s}
  [ "$b" -ne "$len" ] && continue
  out=$(/workspace/dataset/test4_executable "$s" | head -1)
  pred=1; [ "$b" -gt 255 ] && pred=0
  n=$((n+1))
  if [ "$out" != "$pred" ]; then
    fails=$((fails+1))
    printf 'MISMATCH bytes=%d pred=%s got=%s\n' "$b" "$pred" "$out"
    printf '%s' "$s" | od -An -tx1 | head -20
  fi
done
echo "fuzz done: tested=$n mismatches=$fails"

content.text:
Thorough attack complete. The structural half of the rule survived everything; the rule fails on its **lower** bound.

**What survived my attacks** (rule is directionally right):
- Re-ran their many-label evidence: labels=128/bytes=255 → `1`, labels=129/bytes=257 → `0`. Reproduced.
- Re-ran all-dots: 255 dots → `1 0 1 0`, 256 dots → `0 0 1 0`. Reproduced.
- Structural fuzz at fixed lengths 254/255/256 with patterns `.`, `a.`, `..`, `a..`, `.a`, `ab.`, `.a.` — output depends **only** on length, never structure.
- `a*255 + "."`, `"." + a*255`, `a*254 + ".."`, `a*251+".com."` — all 256 bytes, all `0`. No trailing-dot stripping.
- 500-case random-byte fuzz (lengths 1–300, bytes `\x01-\xff`): **0 mismatches** vs a pure byte-length predictor.
- No integer wraparound at 511/512/4096/65535/65536/65791.

**Where it breaks:** the rule states the criterion as "only total byte length" and pins only the upper boundary. It never states a lower bound, and it explicitly claims empty labels have no effect. The empty string — 0 bytes, one empty label — is **rejected**:

```
$ /workspace/dataset/test4_executable ""     ->  0 0 1 0    (rule predicts 1: 0 <= 255)
$ /workspace/dataset/test4_executable "."    ->  1 1 1 0
```

Adding one empty label (`""` → `"."`) flips `is_valid_domain` from 0 to 1, directly contradicting "the presence of empty labels [has] no effect."

I also pinned down a detail the rule leaves ambiguous — the limit is **bytes, not codepoints**, and UTF-8 validity is irrelevant: `85 x U+4F8B` = 255 bytes → `1`, `86 x` = 258 bytes → `0`; `127 x U+00E9` = 254 bytes → `1`, `128 x` = 256 bytes → `0`; `255 x \xff` → `1`, `256 x \xff` → `0`.

input.rule: The number of labels and the presence of empty labels have no effect on is_valid_domain — only total byte length. A string of 255 dots (256 empty labels) is accepted; 256 dots is rejected.
input.counterexample:
Input: "" (the empty string, 0 bytes, i.e. a domain consisting of exactly one empty label).

Command: /workspace/dataset/test4_executable ""

Observed output (4 lines):
0
0
1
0

Predicted by the rule: line1 (is_valid_domain) = 1. The rule says only total byte length matters and that empty labels have no effect; 0 bytes is well under the 255-byte accept threshold it establishes (255 dots accepted, 256 rejected), so the rule predicts acceptance. Observed line1 = 0.

Direct contrast showing the rule's "empty labels have no effect" clause fails:
  /workspace/dataset/test4_executable ""   -> 0 0 1 0   (1 empty label)
  /workspace/dataset/test4_executable "."  -> 1 1 1 0   (2 empty labels)
Adding one empty label flips is_valid_domain from 0 to 1.

Secondary imprecision the rule leaves unstated — the limit is BYTES, not codepoints (rule says "length" without qualifying):
  85 x U+4F8B ($'\xe4\xbe\x8b') = 255 bytes / 85 cp -> 1 0 0 1
  86 x U+4F8B                   = 258 bytes / 86 cp -> 0 0 0 1
  127 x U+00E9 ($'\xc3\xa9')    = 254 bytes /127 cp -> 1 0 0 1
  128 x U+00E9                  = 256 bytes /128 cp -> 0 0 0 1
  255 x $'\xff' (invalid UTF-8) = 255 bytes         -> 1 0 0 1
  256 x $'\xff'                 = 256 bytes         -> 0 0 0 1
input.correctedStatement:
is_valid_domain(s) == (1 <= byte_length(s) <= 255). That is, it is a pure length test on the raw BYTE count of the input, with BOTH an inclusive lower bound of 1 and an inclusive upper bound of 255. The original rule is correct that label structure is irrelevant, but it omits the lower bound and therefore mispredicts the empty string.

Precisely:
- Length is measured in raw bytes, not Unicode codepoints and not grapheme clusters. Verified: 85 x U+4F8B (255 bytes, 85 cp) -> 1 but 86 x U+4F8B (258 bytes) -> 0; 127 x U+00E9 (254 bytes) -> 1 but 128 x U+00E9 (256 bytes) -> 0.
- Content is entirely irrelevant. Every one of the 255 possible single-byte inputs (0x01..0xFF, including LF, CR, TAB, '-', '.', space, and all high bytes) yields is_valid_domain = 1. Malformed UTF-8 (overlong C0 80, surrogate ED A0 80, out-of-range F4 90 80 80) and 255 bytes of 0xFF are all accepted. Leading/trailing dots, consecutive dots, leading/trailing hyphens, underscores, spaces, slashes, and uppercase are all accepted.
- Label structure is genuinely irrelevant at any fixed byte length. At 254, 255 and 256 bytes, the patterns ".", "a.", "..", "a..", ".a", "ab.", ".a." and "abcd." all give identical results, as do "a"x255, "a"x254+".", "."+"a"x254, and ("a."x127)+"a". A 500-case random-byte fuzz (lengths 1-300, alphabet \x01-\xff) produced 0 mismatches against the pure byte-length predictor.
- There is no trailing-dot stripping: "a"x255+"." (256 bytes) -> 0, "a"x251+".com." (256 bytes) -> 0.
- There is no integer truncation/wraparound: lengths 511, 512, 513, 4095, 4096, 65535, 65536, 65537, 65790, 65791, 65792 all -> 0 (tested with both 'a' fill and '.' fill).
- The only rejected input at or below the upper bound is the empty string, and it is rejected because its byte length is 0, not because of its label content.

Caveat for the other three predicates, which the rule does not cover but which share the length dimension: is_valid_label(s) == (1 <= byte_length(s) <= 63) AND s contains no '.' (verified "a"x63 -> 1, "a"x64 -> 0, "" -> 0, "." -> 1 ... note "." itself is length 1 and still yields is_valid_label = 1, so the dot condition needs separate study and is outside this rule's scope).
